unit.title: Use online systems to support managerial decision- making

summary: This unit teaches you to use online systems, such as dashboards, shared files, online surveys and web research, to support management decisions. You will learn to define a decision and its information needs, judge sources and data quality, work out common business measures and expected values, design a dashboard, protect data and logins, and record, communicate and review decisions.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It teaches you to use **online systems** (dashboards, business software, cloud files, online surveys and web research) to get the information a manager needs, check that it can be trusted, and turn it into a sound, recorded decision.

Managers in Jamaican shops, hotels, schools, distribution firms and public bodies now work with live sales screens, shared spreadsheets, email alerts and online reports. The skill is not clicking buttons. It is knowing **which decision you are making, which data it needs, whether the data is good enough, and what the data does not tell you**.
**Who it is for:** supervisors and managers who make or support decisions about staffing, stock, prices, budgets, opening hours, suppliers and services, using information held in online systems.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: State the decision, the questions it raises and the data needed, before opening any system.
Choose the right system (ERP, CRM, dashboard, survey tool, public website) and find reliable information quickly.
Test data for accuracy, completeness, age and consistency, and clean it before analysing.
Work out percentages, rates, averages and expected values correctly; explain what they show and what they do not.
Choose a few measures against targets, use filters, drill-down and alerts, and avoid misleading charts.
Share and edit files with version control, protect logins and personal data, back up and keep an audit trail.
Weigh options and risks, avoid bias, record the reasons, tell the team and check the results later.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with many short scenarios and calculations.
A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms and quick sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical group tasks**: building a dashboard from a data file and using it to justify a decision, and designing and running an online survey. You take a named role and keep screenshots as evidence.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice. Most lost marks in this unit come from percentages of the wrong base (for example dividing by the result instead of the target) and from forgetting the units (J$, per cent, days).
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: From decision to data: working out what you need

blocks.p: Online systems can show hundreds of figures. Without a clear question, a manager either drowns in reports or picks the figures that suit her. The first job is therefore to **define the decision**.

flow: Define the decision and who it affects
List the questions the decision raises
Decide what data would answer each question
Find where that data is held and who owns it
Gather and check the data
Analyse, weigh options and decide
Record, communicate and review

blocks.h: Turning a decision into information needs

head: Decision
Questions to ask
Data needed
Likely online source
rows: Will enough customers come? What will it cost?
Till or POS system, payroll report, online survey
How fast does it sell? How long does delivery take?
Stock system or ERP, supplier portal
Is the new firm real, reliable and cheaper?
Official companies registry search, supplier website, own purchase records
Is it losing money? Do customers value it?

ul: **Relevant**: it bears on this decision.
**Accurate and complete**: right figures, nothing important left out.
**Current**: recent enough for the decision (stock levels need today's data; a yearly trend can use last month's).
**Timely and affordable**: worth the time and cost of getting it. Do not spend a week finding data for a J$5,000 decision.
**Understandable**: in a form the decision maker and the team can read.

blocks.note: A manager who decides first and looks for data afterwards is not using data to decide. She is using it to defend a decision. Define the decision and the criteria (for example 'extra profit of at least J$300,000 a year') before you look at the numbers.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Online** support does not remove the manager's responsibility. The system supplies facts; the manager supplies the question, the checking and the judgement.

sections.title: Online systems and tools managers use

blocks.p: Different systems hold different data. A manager must know which one answers which question, and how fresh its data is.

head: System or tool
What it does
How it helps a decision
rows: Records each sale as it happens
Sales by product, hour, branch and staff member; busy and quiet periods
One system linking purchasing, stock, production, sales, accounts and HR
One set of figures for the whole firm; no re-keying between departments
Records calls, emails, orders, complaints and follow-ups for each customer
Who buys what, who is unhappy, which customers are worth most
Records income, costs, assets, wages and tax
Profit by service, budget against actual, cash position
Shows visits, clicks, orders and when followers are online
Which pages work, when to post or run offers
Collect and summarise answers from customers or staff
Keep files on remote servers that several people can open and edit
Joint budgets, rosters and reports with comments and version history
Pull data from other systems and display key measures
One screen for the main figures; drill-down to detail
Websites of statistics, central bank, registries and regulators
Market size, exchange rates, company registration and industry figures

ul: **Real-time data** is updated the moment a transaction happens. **Batch data** is updated at set times (overnight, weekly). Check the 'last updated' time before you use a report.

**Cloud computing** means software and data run on remote servers reached through the internet. Benefits: access from any place, easy sharing, no firm server to maintain, provider backups. Risks: you need a working connection, data sits with a provider (possibly in another country), subscription costs, and the provider's outage becomes yours.

**Big data** means data sets so large and fast-growing (for example every till transaction of a supermarket chain) that ordinary spreadsheets cannot handle them. Managers usually see the result as a summary in a dashboard.

**Automated and AI tools** can summarise and suggest. Their output must still be checked against the facts, and confidential or personal data must not be pasted into public tools unless the firm's policy allows it.

blocks.note: Island-wide power and internet interruptions happen. A manager who depends on an online system needs a **manual back-up process** (paper forms, a printed stock sheet, an offline copy of key lists) and must tell staff about planned maintenance in good time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A system is only as useful as its users. If a new reporting system has been installed but supervisors still decide from memory, the usual cause is a lack of **training and support**, not the software.

sections.title: Finding and judging online information and running surveys

blocks.p: The internet holds facts, opinions, advertisements and mistakes side by side. When you research a decision such as opening a branch in a town, judge each source.

head: Test
Ask
rows: Who published it? Is it a recognised statistics body, regulator, professional firm or university, or an anonymous page?
How recent is it? Prices, rents and exchange rates go out of date quickly.
Was it written to inform or to sell? An estate agent's advert is not a market study.
Does it say where its figures came from and how they were collected?
Does it cover firms, places and years like yours? A national figure may not fit one parish.

blocks.p: **Primary data** is collected by you for this decision (your own sales records, a survey). **Secondary data** was collected by someone else (published reports, industry figures). Secondary data is faster and cheaper; primary data fits your question better. Most decisions use both.
When comparing your figures with an industry figure, such as staff turnover, check that the other figure covers **similar firms**, is **recent**, and **defines the measure the same way**.

blocks.note: To check whether a possible new supplier is a registered company in Jamaica, use the official companies registry search, not the supplier's own brochure. Also check references and the supplier's delivery record.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Write down the decision and what you need to know
Decide who to ask and how many
Write six to ten short, neutral questions
Add a short purpose note: why, how long, and that no names are collected
Test it with two or three people and fix problems
Send it, remind once, and close on a set date
Export, check and analyse the results

head: Good practice
Poor practice
rows: 'Which closing time suits you best: 6, 7 or 8 p.m.?' (one issue, fixed choices)
'Do you agree that staying open late is a great idea?' (leading)
'How satisfied are you with our prices and service?' (two issues in one)
A balanced scale (very satisfied to very dissatisfied)
A scale with three positive answers and one negative
Anonymous unless names are truly needed

blocks.p: **Response rate** = replies received ÷ surveys sent × 100. If 250 of 1,000 people reply, the response rate is 25%. A low rate raises the risk of **non-response bias**: the people who answer may differ from those who do not (for example only unhappy customers reply, or an online-only survey misses people with poor internet access). Say so when you report the results.

**Percentage who gave an answer** = number giving that answer ÷ number of replies × 100, **not** ÷ number sent. If 300 of the 480 replies say yes, that is 62.5% of replies, not 25% of the 1,200 invited.

blocks.note: A survey result tells you what the people who answered said. It does not tell you what the whole market will do. Use it as one piece of evidence beside sales records and cost figures.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A report can look professional and still be wrong. **Garbage in, garbage out**: poor data produces poor decisions, however good the system. Check quality **before** you analyse, and keep a short **data quality log** of what you found and how you handled it.

head: Quality test
Meaning
Example of failure
rows: Price keyed as J$2,500 instead of J$25,000
Phone-in complaints left out of a complaints report
Overdue accounts report last updated three weeks ago
One branch records dates as day/month, another as month/day
A negative number of guests; a date in the year 2062
Last year's national figures for a local decision

blocks.p: **Data cleansing** (data cleaning) is finding and correcting errors, duplicates and gaps in a data set before analysis.

flow: Copy the original data and keep it unchanged
Look for duplicates, blanks, odd values and mixed formats
Investigate each odd value with the person or system that entered it
Correct, remove or flag it, and write down what you did
Re-check totals against a trusted source
Analyse the cleaned copy

ul: **Odd values (outliers)**: do not delete them just because they are large. A figure ten times the normal level may be a keying error, or a genuine bulk order. Check the source document first.
**Missing values**: find the true figure if possible. Do not guess silently, and say how many were missing.
**Duplicates**: remove only after confirming they are true duplicates (same invoice number, date and amount).
**Totals**: reconcile report totals with another source, such as the bank or accounts figure.

blocks.note: The cause matters as much as the cure. If errors come from staff keying figures by hand, fix the process (drop-down lists, required fields, training), not only the spreadsheet.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Type
Question it answers
Example
rows: Why sales fell in one branch (drill down by product and day)
Staff needed next December, estimated from past sales
The best roster or reorder quantity given costs and limits

head: Measure
Formula
Worked example
rows: Stock on hand ÷ average daily sales
Daily use × delivery lead time (plus a safety margin)
Visits leaving after one page ÷ total visits × 100

blocks.note: A **percentage point** is the plain difference between two percentages. If a sign-up rate rises from 4% to 5.6%, it is up 1.6 percentage points. In relative terms it is up 40% (1.6 ÷ 4). State which you mean.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Comparing options: expected value and decision trees

blocks.p: When outcomes are uncertain, **expected value (EV)** weighs each outcome by its chance: EV = sum of (probability × outcome). Losses count as negatives.

Example: Option X has a 50% chance of J$3,600,000 profit and a 50% chance of a J$800,000 loss. EV = (0.5 × 3,600,000) + (0.5 × −800,000) = 1,800,000 − 400,000 = **J$1,400,000**. Option Y has an 80% chance of J$1,500,000 and a 20% chance of nothing: EV = **J$1,200,000**. A certain J$1,100,000 has an EV of J$1,100,000.
A **decision tree** draws the choices, the chances and the outcomes so the expected values can be worked out and compared. Probabilities on one branch set must add up to 100%.
Expected value is an average over many repeats. A firm that cannot survive a J$800,000 loss may sensibly pick the lower-EV option. EV informs the decision; it does not make it.

blocks.h: Reading trends and avoiding wrong conclusions

ul: Compare **like with like**: December against last December, not against March.
Use a run of figures (a line chart over many weeks), not two single days.
**Correlation is not cause**: sales and temperature may rise together without one causing the other. Test the idea with more data or a trial.
Small numbers mislead: 3 complaints becoming 6 is a 100% rise but may be chance.
Check the **base**: a 20% rise in a tiny branch may be smaller than a 2% rise in a big one.

blocks.p: A **management dashboard** is one screen showing a few key measures at a glance, each against a target, so a manager sees quickly what needs attention.

head: Feature
What it does
Example
rows: Shows actual against target, often with green, amber or red
Shows only part of the data
Only last quarter, only the St Ann branch
Click a total to see the detail behind it
Total sales, then by branch, then by product
Tells the manager only when a figure is outside set limits
Email when a branch's daily cash differs from expected by more than J$10,000

blocks.p: **Management by exception** means the manager spends her time on the figures that are outside limits rather than reading everything.

ul: **Five to eight measures** tied to the unit's goals. Forty measures hide the important ones.
Name the **decision** each measure supports and the **owner** of each target.
Choose the chart for the job: a **line** for change over time, **bars** for comparing branches, a pie only for a few parts of one whole.
Start bar charts at zero. A cut-off axis makes a small difference look large.
Label units and dates, and show when the data was last updated.
Keep colours meaningful (red only for 'off target').
Test it with the real users. If supervisors cannot read it, it is not working.

blocks.p: When a report shows something surprising, such as a branch selling ten times its usual amount, **check the data for an error first**, then investigate the business reason.
If you receive so many reports and alerts that you cannot tell what matters, agree a **few key measures** and set filters and alert limits so that only exceptions reach you.
When data shows a problem, such as most website visitors leaving at the payment page, **investigate the cause** (a fault, a confusing form, a cost shown late) before changing prices or advertising.

sections.title: Working together online: security and data protection

blocks.p: When managers in several towns build one budget, use **one shared file** with comments and version history. Two people editing separate copies produces figures that do not match. Agree who owns the file, how changes are made, and which version is final.

head: Risk
Control
rows: Strong, unique passwords; **two-factor authentication** (password plus a code on a phone) so a stolen password alone is not enough
**Phishing**: a fake email or message that tries to trick you into giving passwords or details
Do not click links asking you to 'confirm' a password; go to the site yourself; report it to IT or the security officer
Staff seeing data they do not need
**Access control**: each person opens only the data their job requires (need to know, least privilege); review access when people change roles or leave
Regular **backups** kept separately, including one off-site or in a different cloud location; test that they can be restored
An **audit trail**: a time-stamped log of who did what in the system
Follow the firm's policy; do not copy customer or staff data to personal phones or flash drives
Avoid sensitive work on open networks; lock screens; report lost devices at once

blocks.p: Jamaica's **data protection law** sets rules for how organisations collect, use, store and share information about identifiable people (customers, staff, patients, students). In practice: collect only what you need, say why, keep it accurate, keep it secure, do not keep it longer than needed, and share it only for proper reasons. Staff salary and customer records are personal data, so access is limited to those whose role requires it.

blocks.note: Before downloading customers' personal data to analyse at home, stop and check the data protection law and the firm's policy. Convenience is not a reason to move personal data to an uncontrolled device. Where possible use anonymised or summary data.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: A tool that works in one country may store data in another. Ask the IT officer where a cloud service keeps the firm's data before relying on it for personal or sensitive records.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Making, recording, communicating and reviewing decisions

ul: List **options**, including 'do nothing'.
Agree **criteria** (profit, cost, risk, customer effect, staff effect, time).
Use a **weighted scoring** table, **cost-benefit** figures or **expected values**, whichever fits.
Test **'what if'**: what happens if sales are 20% lower or costs 10% higher?
Think about **risk**: can the firm survive the worst case?

head: Trap
What happens
Defence
rows: You look only for figures that support what you already believe
Search for evidence against your view; ask a colleague to challenge it
You give too much weight to last week
Use a longer run of data
The first figure you see sets your thinking
Work out your own estimate first
You follow a recommendation without checking why
Check the reasons; add what the system cannot know (local events, supplier problems, staff views)
You continue because money is already spent
Judge only future costs and benefits

blocks.p: If a system recommends dropping a popular product because sales fell last month, check the **reasons** (a stock-out, a price change, a holiday week) and use judgement as well as the data.

Keep a **decision record** in the online system: the decision, date, decision maker, data used and its limits, options considered, reasons, risks, who will act, and the **review date**. If the decision is questioned later, the record shows how and why it was made.

ul: Tell the team **what** was decided, **why** and **which data** supports it.
Give each task an owner and a date.
Plan for downtime: a manual process and notice to staff.
Provide training so staff can use the new reports and tools.

blocks.p: Set the measures and the date for review at the time you decide. Three months after changing delivery routes, for example, compare the actual results with the expected gains. If results differ, find out why, adjust, and record the lesson.

flow: Decide and record
Set the measures and review date
Collect the results
Compare with the expected gains
Adjust and record the lesson

ul: state the decision and list the data it needs before I open any system
say which online system holds which kind of data, and when its data was last updated
judge an online source for who, when, why, how and match
design a short, neutral, anonymous online survey and work out its response rate
test data for accuracy, completeness, age, consistency and duplicates, and clean it with a log
name the four types of analytics and give an example of each
work out percentage of target, percentage change, conversion, average order value, days of stock, bounce rate and expected value
design a dashboard of a few measures against targets, with filters, drill-down and alerts
use shared files with version control, two-factor login, access control, backups and an audit trail
recognise phishing and protect personal data under the data protection law
avoid confirmation bias and over-reliance on systems, and use judgement with data
record a decision, communicate it, and review its results against what was expected

terms: Data updated the moment a transaction happens.
Finding and correcting errors, duplicates and gaps before analysis.
One screen of key measures, each against a target.
Clicking a total to see the detail behind it.
Giving attention only to figures outside set limits.
Enterprise resource planning: one system linking purchasing, stock, production, sales and accounts.
Customer relationship management: a system recording contacts with customers.
Orders (or sign-ups) as a percentage of visits.
Share of visitors who leave after viewing one page.
Showing two versions to different visitors and comparing results.
Replies received as a percentage of surveys sent.
Sum of each outcome multiplied by its probability.
A diagram of choices, chances and outcomes.
Login needing a password plus a second check.
A fake message designed to steal passwords or details.
A time-stamped log of who did what in a system.
Each person can open only the data their job needs.
A separate copy of data that can be restored after loss.
Software and data running on remote servers reached by internet.
Data sets too large and fast-growing for ordinary tools.
Looking only for evidence that supports what you already believe.

c1.title: An online ordering page for a Falmouth bakery
c1.text: Natalie Reid manages online ordering for a bakery group based in Falmouth. Last week her website had 5,200 visits and 195 orders worth J$487,500 in total. She tested two versions of the order page by showing each to 1,500 different visitors: version A produced 60 sign-ups for the loyalty club and version B produced 84. Her analytics also show that 2,080 of the 5,200 visits ended after one page.

c2.title: A stock report at a Black River hardware store
c2.text: Winston Gayle manages a hardware store in Black River whose stock system updates as each sale is made. The system shows 900 bags of a popular tile adhesive on hand, selling about 45 bags a day. The supplier takes 14 days to deliver. While checking the monthly sales report, Winston finds the same invoice number entered twice, six sales with no date, and one item priced at J$1,250 when the shelf price is J$12,500.

c3.title: A municipal corporation's service survey
c3.text: A municipal corporation in St Catherine uses an online system to log garbage-collection complaints and sent an online survey to 2,000 ratepayers on its email and text list. 340 replied and 255 of those said they were satisfied. The revenue officer wants to export the survey file, with names and phone numbers, to her home laptop to prepare a presentation.

c4.title: Security in a Linstead distribution firm
c4.text: Andre Wright manages a distribution firm in Linstead. Three sales staff share one login to the sales system. An email that appears to come from IT says that the mailbox is full and asks staff to click a link and re-enter their passwords. Two managers have each edited their own copy of the price list. Andre also keeps the customer list on his personal phone so that he can work on weekends.

c5.title: A tour operator's new-product decision in Port Antonio
c5.text: Simone Walters runs a small tour company in Port Antonio and must choose one of three plans. Plan X: 50% chance of a J$3,600,000 profit and 50% chance of a J$800,000 loss. Plan Y: 80% chance of a J$1,500,000 profit and 20% chance of no profit. Plan Z: a certain profit of J$1,100,000. She already believes Plan X is best and has begun collecting only the booking figures that favour it. The company's reserves could not cover a J$800,000 loss.

questions.q: What was the website's conversion rate for the week?
questions.why: Conversion rate = orders ÷ visits × 100 = 195 ÷ 5,200 × 100 = 3.75%. Dividing by orders or moving the decimal point gives the other values.

questions.q: What was the average order value?
questions.why: Average order value = total sales ÷ number of orders = J$487,500 ÷ 195 = J$2,500. Check: 195 × 2,500 = 487,500.

questions.q: How much higher was the sign-up rate of version B than version A?
o: 24 sign-ups per hundred
40 percentage points
1.6 percentage points
questions.why: A is 60 ÷ 1,500 = 4.0% and B is 84 ÷ 1,500 = 5.6%, a difference of 1.6 percentage points (a 40% relative rise). A difference between two percentages is stated in percentage points.

questions.q: What does the bounce rate of the bakery's website show?
o: 40% of visitors bought something
40% of visits ended after one page
40 visits ended in an error
40% of orders were cancelled
questions.why: Bounce rate = 2,080 ÷ 5,200 × 100 = 40%: the share of visits that left after one page. It says nothing about orders. The manager would investigate the pages with the highest exit rates.

questions.q: About how many days of stock of the adhesive does Winston have?
o: 14 days
20 days
6 days
45 days
questions.why: Days of stock = stock ÷ daily sales = 900 ÷ 45 = 20 days. The delivery time of 14 days is a separate figure that must be compared with it.

questions.q: When should Winston reorder, if his reorder point is daily use multiplied by the supplier's lead time?
o: When stock falls to 450 bags
When stock reaches zero
When stock falls to 900 bags
When stock falls to 630 bags
questions.why: Reorder point = 45 × 14 = 630 bags, so the new stock arrives as the old stock runs down. With 900 on hand, that point is reached in 6 days. Waiting for zero would cause a stock-out.

questions.q: What should Winston do first about the item priced at J$1,250 instead of J$12,500?
o: Check the source document and correct the entry
Delete the whole record so the totals are not affected
Leave it, because one item does not matter
Change the shelf price to match the system
questions.why: Odd values are checked against the source (invoice or price list) before they are corrected, and the correction is recorded in a data quality log. Deleting records loses true sales, and one wrong price can distort the report totals.

questions.q: What was the survey's response rate?
questions.why: Response rate = replies ÷ surveys sent × 100 = 340 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 17%. The 75% figure is the share of replies that were satisfied (255 ÷ 340).

questions.q: What percentage of those who replied said they were satisfied?
questions.why: 255 ÷ 340 × 100 = 75% of the replies. The base is the people who answered, not the 2,000 invited. Using 2,000 would give 12.75%.

questions.q: Which is the most important limit to state when reporting the survey result?
o: Only 17% replied, and some ratepayers were never asked
The survey was done online, not on paper
Satisfied replies were 75%, which is too high to use
The survey asked about garbage collection only
questions.why: A low response rate and a list that leaves out ratepayers without contact details mean the replies may not represent all ratepayers (non-response and coverage bias). The result is useful evidence but must be reported with this limit.

questions.q: What should the revenue officer do about taking the survey file with names and phone numbers home?
o: Take it home, because it is needed for official work
Email it to her private account to keep it safe
Copy it to a friend's computer to get a second opinion
Use anonymised results and follow the law and policy
questions.why: Personal data must be protected and kept on controlled systems. For a presentation, anonymised or summary figures are enough. Moving the file to personal devices breaks the data protection law and the policy.

questions.q: What is the biggest problem with three staff sharing one login?
o: The system will run more slowly for all users
The audit trail cannot show who did what
It uses up more of the firm's software licence
It forces everyone to make passwords longer
questions.why: An audit trail records the actions of each user. With a shared login, nobody can be held accountable and access cannot be limited by role. Each person needs a personal account with the access the job requires.

questions.q: What should staff do about the email asking them to re-enter their passwords?
o: Click the link to see whether the page looks genuine
Not click, and report it as likely phishing
Reply with the old password to prove who they are
Forward it to all colleagues as a warning with the link intact
questions.why: A genuine IT department does not ask for passwords by email. Phishing relies on a link to a fake page. Staff should not click, should report it to IT, and should go to the system by its usual address if worried.

questions.q: What would have prevented the mismatch between the two managers' price lists?
o: Emailing the file between the two managers every day
A longer password on each copy
Printing the list each week
One shared file with version control
questions.why: Version control in a single shared file means everyone edits the same current version and changes can be traced. Separate copies will drift apart however often they are emailed.

questions.q: Which action best reduces the risk of a stolen password being used to enter the sales system?
o: Two-factor authentication
Changing the screen colour
A larger monitor
Locking the office door
questions.why: With two-factor authentication a thief needs the second check (such as a code sent to the user's phone) as well as the password. Physical locks do not stop remote logins.

questions.q: Which plan has the highest expected value?
o: Plan Y, at J$1,200,000
Plan Z, at J$1,100,000
Plan X, at J$1,400,000
Plan X, at J$2,800,000

questions.q: Simone's reserves cannot cover a J$800,000 loss. What is the sound way to use the figures?
o: Choose Plan X, because the highest expected value always wins
Choose the plan with the largest possible profit
Weigh the risk of loss too, and consider Plan Y or Z
Ignore the reserves, because they are not data
questions.why: Expected value is an average over many repeats. A firm that cannot survive the worst case may sensibly accept a lower expected value for lower risk. Reserves are an important fact for the decision.

questions.q: Simone collects only the booking figures that favour Plan X. What is this error called, and what is the fix?
o: Confirmation bias; look for evidence against Plan X too
Anchoring; wait until a competitor has made its own decision
Recency bias; base the choice only on last week's bookings
Sunk cost; spend more on research into Plan X to be sure
questions.why: Looking only for supporting evidence is confirmation bias. The defence is to search for evidence against the preferred option, test 'what if' cases, and ask a colleague to challenge the analysis.

questions.q: A manager's dashboard shows 28 measures, and she misses a fall in one that matters. What is the best change?
o: Add an alert for each of the 28 measures
Print the dashboard in a smaller font
Remove all targets from the dashboard
Cut it to a few measures tied to key goals
questions.why: A dashboard works when it highlights the few measures tied to goals, with a target and an owner. More alerts or smaller print increase the clutter.

questions.q: A weekly report shows that sales of one product doubled in a single week. What should a manager check before ordering twice as much stock?
o: Whether the supplier offers a larger pallet size
Whether it was a one-off event or a lasting trend
Whether competitors also stock the same product
Whether the report was printed or viewed on screen
questions.why: A one-week jump may come from a promotion, a holiday, a bulk buyer or a keying error. Ordering from one week of data repeats a possible mistake. Check the cause and look at a longer run of figures before deciding.
